question: According to official EU data, 41.6 % of households in the EU experienced at least some difficulty getting by in 2024.

Declining personal incomes, the high cost of basic items, soaring rents, energy poverty, the degradation and commercialisation of health and social support for children, the elderly and people with disabilities – these factors all contribute to the mounting insecurity faced by young couples looking to start a family.

The debate on this subject in Greece and in other EU Member States reflects the ‘concern’ of national governments and the EU institutions with regard to the trend of the declining working-age population, giving rise to corresponding policies for managing low birth rates. How does the European Commission respond to: 1.

the fact that the EU’s anti-labour policy forms precarious employment conditions with flexible forms of employment (such as zero-hour and work-on-demand contracts), negatively affecting female workers in particular and creating barriers for young couples to having a child?

the fact that, over time, EU and national government policies have resulted in the commodification of early childhood education and care, creative activities for children, special education and comprehensive child protection – instead of these being universal rights for every child – as part of a wider trend of commercialisation and privatisation, as seen in the areas of housing, water and energy?

the fact that policy of commodifying healthcare, including prenatal care and medically assisted reproduction, has created a field of business activity resulting in unaffordable costs for young couples?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.1.2026) The Commission actions are guided by the European Pillar of Social Rights (EPSR) which also promotes fair working conditions, the right to access early childhood education and care (ECEC) and timely access to affordable, preventive and curative healthcare of good quality.

Directive 2019/11521 sets out minimum requirements promoting transparent and predictable working conditions. Directive 2003/882 lays down minimum requirements for the protection of the health and safety of workers by regulating working time. Alongside the Work-life balance Directive3, these instruments reflect fair working conditions principles from the EPSR and rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundaments Rights4.

The EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child sets out a framework to protect the rights of all children, supported by the Council Recommendations establishing a European Child Guarantee5 and on Early Childhood Education and Care: Barcelona targets for 20306 and the Commission Recommendation on integrated child protection systems7.

While their implementation lies within the remits of national competences, the Commission supports it, including through funding8 and monitoring. The Roadmap on Women’s Rights9 promotes women’s health, including antenatal care, sexual and reproductive health, respecting Member States’ competence to organise their health systems.
In line with the EPSR, the Commission supports the Member States including through the EU4Health programme10, and facilitating the exchange of good practices.
